items.topic: Classification and effects of water pollutants
items.question_md:
Assertion (A): Heavy metal pollution from mining can enter the food chain through bioaccumulation.

Reason (R): Metals like mercury, cadmium, and arsenic cannot be metabolized or excreted efficiently by organisms.

(a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
(c) A is true, R is false
(d) A is false, R is true
items.answer_md: **(a)** Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Mercury, cadmium and arsenic are not broken down or excreted quickly, so they accumulate in tissue (bioaccumulation) and are passed up the food chain, increasing in concentration at each trophic level (biomagnification).

items.question_md: Is eutrophication healthy or unhealthy for lakes? Lake A receives untreated sewage, while Lake B receives only agricultural runoffs rich in nutrients. Which lake is more likely to experience faster eutrophication, and why? [Max 35-40 words]
items.answer_md: Eutrophication is **unhealthy**: nutrient enrichment causes algal blooms, which die and decay, depleting dissolved oxygen and killing fish. **Lake A** eutrophicates faster because untreated sewage carries nitrogen and phosphorus plus a heavy organic load, so decay also consumes oxygen directly (high BOD).

items.question_md:
Write balanced chemical reactions for the formation of inorganic particulate matter (PMs) by mentioning the processes (heat or combustion) involved therein.
(i) Coal Containing Pyrite
(ii) Coal Containing Limestone
(iii) Automobiles Containing Leaded Gasoline
items.answer_md:
**(i) Coal containing pyrite (combustion):** pyrite is oxidised to iron(III) oxide, which leaves as fly ash, and $SO_2$ gas.
$$4FeS_2 + 11O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{combustion}} 2Fe_2O_3 + 8SO_2$$

**(ii) Coal containing limestone (heat):** limestone is calcined; the lime formed is carried out as fine particulate (and can also capture $SO_2$ as sulphite/sulphate particles).
$$CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} CaO + CO_2$$
$$CaO + SO_2 \rightarrow CaSO_3,\quad 2CaSO_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2CaSO_4$$

**(iii) Automobiles with leaded gasoline (combustion):** the antiknock additive tetraethyl lead burns to lead oxide; with the scavenger ethylene dibromide it forms volatile $PbBr_2$ that condenses into fine lead-halide particles in the exhaust.
$$2Pb(C_2H_5)_4 + 27O_2 \rightarrow 2PbO + 16CO_2 + 20H_2O$$
$$PbO + C_2H_4Br_2 \rightarrow PbBr_2 + \text{(organic products)}$$

items.question_md: How does deforestation contribute to global warming? [Max 25-30 words]
items.answer_md: Trees absorb $CO_2$ by photosynthesis. Cutting and burning or decaying them removes this sink and releases stored carbon as $CO_2$, raising the greenhouse effect and so global warming.

items.topic: Control of gaseous and particulate pollutants
items.question_md: For soot/dust/aerosol control, which scrubber is preferable between dry and wet scrubbers and why? Give one real-world example of each used in air pollution control. [Max 35-40 words]
items.answer_md: A **wet scrubber** is preferable for soot, dust and aerosols: water droplets capture fine particles and also absorb soluble gases (e.g. $SO_2$), and sticky or explosive dust is handled safely. Its drawback is sludge and wastewater. Example: venturi scrubber on steel-plant/thermal-plant flue gas. A **dry scrubber** injects dry lime or sorbent and gives dry waste with no water; example: lime-injection / spray-dryer absorber in coal power plants.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/2025-2026 Papers/Mid Term 2025-26 Sem 1 ALL.pdf
items.question_md: Identify the atmospheric layer that is referred to by two names and mention them. Why does the temperature increase sharply with altitude in the thermosphere layer? [Max 45-50 words]
items.answer_md: The **thermosphere** is also called the **ionosphere** (it contains the ionised layers, and extends from about 80 km upward). Temperature rises sharply with altitude because the very thin gas there (mainly $O_2$ and $N_2$) absorbs highly energetic solar X-rays and extreme UV (wavelengths below about 200 nm), which ionises and dissociates molecules and gives the few particles very high kinetic energy, up to 1500 degrees C or more.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/2025-2026 Papers/Mid Term 2025-26 Sem 1 ALL.pdf
items.question_md: How the concentration (in ppm) of NO, $NO_2$, and $O_2$ gas changes with time (0:00 to 24:00 hr). Also, explain this by sketching a diagram. [Max 45-50 words]
items.answer_md:
This is the diurnal pattern of photochemical smog. (Ozone is the secondary product, so the third curve is normally $O_3$; the paper prints $O_2$, which stays essentially constant.)

**Diagram (concentration in ppm vs time, 0 to 24 h):** NO peaks sharply in the morning rush hour (about 6-9 h) and falls to near zero by midday; $NO_2$ rises as NO is oxidised, peaks a little after NO (about 8-10 h), dips at noon and shows a smaller evening peak; $O_3$ stays low at night, rises after sunrise, peaks in the early afternoon (about 12-15 h) and falls after sunset.

**Explanation:**
$$NO_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} NO + O,\qquad O + O_2 \rightarrow O_3,\qquad NO + O_3 \rightarrow NO_2 + O_2$$
Traffic emits NO in the morning; sunlight photolyses $NO_2$ and drives ozone formation (with hydrocarbons giving PAN and aldehydes) to a midday maximum; at night, with no sunlight, ozone is consumed by NO and the cycle resets. Atmospheric $O_2$ stays about constant (about 210000 ppm).

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/2025-2026 Papers/Mid Term 2025-26 Sem 1 ALL.pdf
items.question_md: What is the tactic behind the Fractional Distillation Approach? Draw an evident layout and explain why it is used in petroleum refining from crude oil. Compose at least one environmental concern linked with this process? [Max 65-70 words]
items.answer_md:
**Principle:** crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different boiling points. It is heated to about 350-400 degrees C in a furnace and the vapour enters a tall fractionating column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Each component rises until the temperature falls below its boiling point, condenses on a tray and is drawn off.

**Layout (draw):** furnace feeding the column near the bottom; trays with bubble caps; outlets from top to bottom: refinery gas (below 40 degrees C), petrol/gasoline (40-180), kerosene (180-250), diesel/gas oil (250-350), lubricating oil and fuel oil, and bitumen/residue at the bottom, with temperature falling upward.

**Why used:** it separates the mixture continuously and on a large scale into useful fractions with different uses (fuels, lubricants, petrochemical feedstock, road tar) without chemical change, using differences in boiling point.

**Environmental concern:** burning refinery fuel and flaring release $CO_2$, $SO_2$ and $NO_x$ (air pollution, acid rain, global warming); also oily wastewater and spills contaminate water bodies, and VOC leaks form smog.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: How do emissions of halogen source gases lead to Stratospheric ozone depletion?
items.answer_md:
Halogen source gases (CFCs, halons, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$, $\mathrm{CH_3CCl_3}$) are inert in the troposphere, so they reach the stratosphere, where UV releases Cl or Br atoms: $\mathrm{CF_2Cl_2 + h\nu \rightarrow CF_2Cl^\bullet + Cl^\bullet}$.

These atoms destroy ozone catalytically: $\mathrm{Cl^\bullet + O_3 \rightarrow ClO^\bullet + O_2}$; $\mathrm{ClO^\bullet + O \rightarrow Cl^\bullet + O_2}$ (net $\mathrm{O_3 + O \rightarrow 2O_2}$). Cl is regenerated, so one atom destroys about $10^5$ $\mathrm{O_3}$ molecules.

items.question_md: Differentiate between two-way and three-way Catalytic Converter.
items.answer_md:
| Two-way catalytic converter | Three-way catalytic converter |
|---|---|
| Removes **two** pollutants: CO and HC (oxidation only) | Removes **three**: CO, HC and $\mathrm{NO_x}$ (oxidation + reduction) |
| $\mathrm{2CO + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2}$; $\mathrm{HC + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O}$ | also $\mathrm{2NO + 2CO \rightarrow N_2 + 2CO_2}$ |
| Catalyst Pt and Pd | Pt, Pd **and Rh** (Rh reduces $\mathrm{NO_x}$) |
| Works with excess air; used in diesel and older petrol engines | Needs air-fuel ratio near stoichiometric (about 14.7:1), controlled by an oxygen ($\lambda$) sensor |

items.question_md: Explain the principle behind Electrostatic Precipitators to remove air pollution.
items.answer_md:
**Principle**: dust particles are charged by a **corona discharge** and then attracted to an oppositely charged collecting surface.

A high negative DC voltage (30-100 kV) on thin wires ionises the gas around them; the negative ions attach to particles, the charged particles move to the earthed collecting plates, and the collected dust is rapped off into a hopper. Efficiency is above 99% even for particles of about 0.1 µm.

items.question_md: Explain relative effects of all the five Greenhouse gases. Also discuss the consequences of Global Warming on all the life forms and Environment.
items.answer_md:
**Greenhouse gases (GHGs)** trap outgoing infrared radiation from the Earth and re-emit it downward, warming the surface. Their relative effect depends on concentration, how strongly each molecule absorbs IR (**Global Warming Potential, GWP**, relative to $\mathrm{CO_2}$ = 1 over 100 years) and lifetime.

| GHG | Main sources | GWP (100 yr, IPCC AR5) | Approx. share of enhanced warming |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | fossil fuels, deforestation, cement | 1 | ~60% (largest because of huge amount) |
| $\mathrm{CH_4}$ | paddy fields, cattle, landfills, natural gas leaks | ~28 | ~20% |
| CFCs (CFC-11, CFC-12) | refrigerants, aerosols, foams | ~4,700-10,200 | ~14% |
| $\mathrm{N_2O}$ | nitrogen fertilisers, combustion | ~265 | ~6% |
| Tropospheric $\mathrm{O_3}$ | photochemical smog | short-lived, regional | small, variable |

(Water vapour is the most abundant natural GHG but acts as a feedback, not a direct human emission.) So $\mathrm{CO_2}$ contributes most in total, while per molecule CFCs > $\mathrm{N_2O}$ > $\mathrm{CH_4}$ > $\mathrm{CO_2}$.

**Consequences of global warming**
- **Environment**: rise in global mean temperature (about 1.1 °C above pre-industrial); melting of glaciers and polar ice; sea-level rise flooding coastal areas and islands; more frequent heat waves, droughts, floods and cyclones; changed monsoon pattern.
- **Plants and agriculture**: shift of crop belts, lower yields of wheat and rice from heat stress, more pests and weeds.
- **Animals and ecosystems**: coral bleaching from warm and acidified oceans; species migrating poleward or uphill; extinction of species that cannot adapt (polar bears, amphibians).
- **Humans**: heat stroke, spread of vector-borne diseases (malaria, dengue) to new areas, water scarcity, food insecurity and climate refugees.

items.question_md: Differentiate between Biological oxygen demand (BOD) and Chemical oxygen demand (COD).
items.answer_md:
| BOD | COD |
|---|---|
| Oxygen needed by **microorganisms** to oxidise biodegradable organic matter | Oxygen equivalent of organic matter oxidised **chemically** by acidic $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$ |
| Measures only biodegradable matter | Measures biodegradable + non-biodegradable matter |
| Takes 5 days at 20 °C | Takes about 2-3 h |
| Affected by toxic substances that kill microbes | Not affected by toxicity |
| Value is lower | Value is higher: **COD ≥ BOD** |

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.topic: Classification and effects of water pollutants
items.question_md: Discuss the classification of water pollutants in detail with suitable examples.
items.answer_md:
Water pollutants are substances or forms of energy that make water harmful for its use. They are classified as follows.

## 1. Organic pollutants
- **Oxygen-demanding (biodegradable) wastes**: sewage, food-processing, dairy, paper and sugar wastes; microbes decompose them using dissolved oxygen, raising **BOD** and killing fish.
- **Synthetic organics**: pesticides (DDT, BHC), detergents, phenols, PCBs, plastics and dyes; many are non-biodegradable and cause **biomagnification** and toxicity.
- **Oil**: spills from tankers and refineries form a surface film that cuts oxygen exchange and kills birds and marine life.

## 2. Inorganic pollutants
- **Heavy metals**: Hg (Minamata disease), Cd (itai-itai disease), Pb, As (arsenicosis in West Bengal), Cr; toxic and bioaccumulative.
- **Acids, alkalis and salts**: acid mine drainage, industrial effluents; change pH and salinity.
- **Fluoride** above 1.5 mg/L causes fluorosis.

## 3. Plant nutrients
Nitrates and phosphates from fertilizer runoff, sewage and detergents cause **eutrophication** and algal blooms; nitrate causes **blue baby syndrome**.

## 4. Pathogens (biological pollutants)
Bacteria, viruses, protozoa and worms from sewage and animal waste cause cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis and jaundice. Indicator: coliform count.

## 5. Sediments and suspended solids
Silt and clay from soil erosion, mining and construction increase **turbidity**, cut light penetration, clog fish gills and silt up reservoirs.

## 6. Radioactive pollutants
Radioisotopes ($\mathrm{^{90}Sr}$, $\mathrm{^{131}I}$, $\mathrm{^{137}Cs}$) from nuclear plants, mining and medical use cause cancer and genetic damage.

## 7. Thermal pollution (heat)
Hot cooling water from power plants lowers dissolved oxygen and harms temperature-sensitive aquatic organisms.

**Classification by source**: point sources (industrial outfalls, sewage pipes) and non-point sources (agricultural runoff, urban storm water).

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md:
Explain the following for Trickling Filters as Secondary Treatment of Wastewater:

a) objective

b) principle

c) well-labelled diagram

d) functioning
\ne) advantages and disadvantages over other Secondary Treatment processes.
items.answer_md:
**a) Objective:** to remove dissolved and colloidal biodegradable organic matter (BOD) from primary-treated sewage by aerobic biological oxidation, producing an effluent of low BOD and suspended solids.

**b) Principle:** **attached-growth aerobic oxidation**. Microorganisms grow as a slime layer (biofilm) on the media; as sewage trickles over it, they adsorb and oxidise the organics using oxygen from air in the voids:
$$\text{Organics} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{microbes}} \mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \text{new cells}$$
It is a biological reactor, not a mechanical strainer.

**c) Well-labelled diagram (described):** circular tank with a **central feed pipe**, **rotating distributor arms**, **filter media** (crushed stone/plastic, 25-75 mm, 1-2.5 m deep) carrying the **biological film**, **underdrain system** with **ventilation ports**, **effluent outlet** to the **secondary settling tank**, and a **recirculation line**.

**d) Functioning:**
1. Settled sewage is sprayed by the rotating arm over the media.
2. It trickles down in thin films; air rises by natural draft.
3. The biofilm oxidises organic matter (and nitrifies $\mathrm{NH_3}$ in lower layers).
4. The film thickens, its inner layer turns anaerobic and **sloughs off**; the sloughed humus is removed in the secondary clarifier.
5. Effluent may be recirculated to dilute strong sewage and keep the media wet.

**e) Advantages and disadvantages over other secondary processes (e.g. ASP):**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| Simple, little skill needed | Lower BOD removal (65-90% vs 85-95% for ASP) |
| Low power (no forced aeration) | Needs larger area and head loss |
| Withstands shock and toxic loads | Odour and filter-fly nuisance |
| No sludge bulking problem | Clogging/ponding of media |
| Less sludge produced | Performance falls in cold weather |

items.question_md: Describe the sources of noise pollution in brief.
items.answer_md:
**Sources of noise pollution**
1. **Transport**: road traffic and horns, motorbikes, trains, aircraft (the main urban source).
2. **Industrial**: machines, generators, compressors, mills.
3. **Construction**: drilling, pile driving, concrete mixers, blasting.
4. **Social and domestic**: loudspeakers, DJs, firecrackers, festivals, TV, music systems, coolers and DG sets.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Why continental crust has risen up whereas oceanic crust has dipped down?
items.answer_md:
Because of **isostasy**: both crusts "float" on the denser, plastic mantle, and each sinks to a depth set by its density and thickness.

- **Continental crust** is **granitic** (rich in Si and Al, "sial"), **lighter** (density ~2.7 g/cm³) and **thicker** (30-70 km), so it floats high and stands above sea level.
- **Oceanic crust** is **basaltic** (rich in Si and Mg, "sima"), **denser** (~3.0 g/cm³) and **thinner** (5-10 km), so it sits lower and forms the ocean basins. Where the two plates collide, the denser oceanic plate is the one that **subducts** (dips down) beneath the continental plate.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Explain how freezing is responsible for the formation of soil.
items.answer_md: Water entering cracks of rocks freezes below 0 °C and **expands by about 9% in volume**, exerting large pressure that widens the cracks (**frost wedging**). Repeated **freeze-thaw cycles** break the rock into smaller fragments; this physical weathering of parent rock produces the mineral particles from which soil is formed.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss the steps by which soil pollution can be prevented.
items.answer_md:
**Steps to prevent soil pollution**

1. **Judicious use of agrochemicals**: apply fertilisers only after soil testing; use biofertilisers (*Rhizobium*, *Azotobacter*, blue-green algae), compost and vermicompost.
2. **Integrated pest management**: biological control, biopesticides (neem), crop rotation; ban persistent pesticides such as DDT.
3. **Proper solid-waste management**: segregation at source, reduce-reuse-recycle, composting of wet waste, and disposal only in **sanitary landfills** with liners and leachate collection instead of open dumps.
4. **Treatment of industrial waste**: effluents and sludge must be treated (ETP) before discharge; hazardous waste goes to secure landfills (Hazardous Waste Rules 2016).
5. **Reduce plastics**: ban single-use plastics, recycle, use biodegradable alternatives.
6. **Safe irrigation**: avoid untreated sewage or saline water; provide drainage to prevent salinity.
7. **Afforestation and soil conservation**: tree cover, contour ploughing and terracing prevent erosion and keep pollutants in place.
8. **Remediation of polluted land**: bioremediation (microbes), phytoremediation (plants), liming acidic soils, gypsum for sodic soils, reclamation of mined land.
9. **Laws and awareness**: enforce the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and waste rules; educate farmers and citizens.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Differentiate between Pyramids of Numbers and Pyramids of Biomass.
items.answer_md:
| Pyramid of numbers | Pyramid of biomass |
|---|---|
| Shows the **number of individuals** at each trophic level | Shows the **total dry mass** (g/m²) of organisms at each trophic level |
| Ignores size: one large tree counts the same as one grass plant | Takes size into account |
| Upright (grassland), inverted (parasitic chain) or spindle-shaped (tree ecosystem) | Upright on land, **inverted in aquatic** ecosystems (phytoplankton < zooplankton) |
| Example: grass (many) → grasshoppers → frogs → snake (one) | Example: forest trees (large biomass) → herbivores → carnivores |

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What does Biogeochemical cycles mean? Explain their importance in Ecology and state in what respect Sulphur cycle is different from all other Biogeochemical cycles?
items.answer_md:
### Meaning
**Biogeochemical cycles** are the cyclic pathways by which chemical elements (C, N, O, P, S, H, water) move from the abiotic environment (atmosphere, lithosphere, hydrosphere) into living organisms and back again, through biological, geological and chemical processes. They are **gaseous** (N, C, O) or **sedimentary** (P, S).

### Importance in ecology
1. **Recycle limited nutrients:** the Earth is a closed system for matter; recycling makes the finite stock of nutrients available again and again.
2. **Link biotic and abiotic components** and keep ecosystems functioning; energy flows one way but matter cycles.
3. **Maintain balance** of gases in the atmosphere ($\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{N_2}$) and regulate climate.
4. **Support productivity:** supply N, P, S needed for proteins, nucleic acids and ATP.
5. **Decompose and detoxify wastes** through decomposers.
6. Their disturbance by humans causes eutrophication, acid rain, global warming.

### How the sulphur cycle differs from other cycles
1. It is a **mixed cycle**: mainly **sedimentary** (reservoir in rocks: gypsum, pyrite, and ocean sulphate) but it also has a **gaseous phase** ($\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, DMS), unlike phosphorus (no gas) or nitrogen (mainly gas).
2. It involves **many oxidation states** (-2 in $\mathrm{H_2S}$, 0 in S, +4 in $\mathrm{SO_2}$, +6 in $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$), driven by specialised bacteria: sulphur-oxidising (*Thiobacillus*, $\mathrm{H_2S \rightarrow S \rightarrow SO_4^{2-}}$) and sulphate-reducing (*Desulfovibrio*, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow H_2S}$).
3. Its atmospheric part is strongly **affected by human activity** (fossil-fuel combustion) and leads to **acid rain**: $\mathrm{2SO_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2SO_3},\ \mathrm{SO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_4}$.
4. It is closely **coupled with the iron and carbon cycles** (formation of pyrite $\mathrm{FeS_2}$ in anaerobic sediments).

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: Discuss Nitrogen Cycle by detailed description of Nitrogen Fixation, Assimilation, Nitrification, Denitrification and Ammonification. Also draw properly labelled diagram.
items.answer_md:
Nitrogen forms 78% of air but most organisms cannot use $\mathrm{N_2}$ directly. The nitrogen cycle converts it into usable forms and back.

### 1. Nitrogen fixation
Conversion of $\mathrm{N_2}$ into $\mathrm{NH_3}$/nitrates.
- **Biological:** *Rhizobium* (legume root nodules), *Azotobacter*, *Clostridium*, cyanobacteria (*Anabaena*, *Nostoc*) using nitrogenase:
$$\mathrm{N_2 + 8H^+ + 8e^- + 16ATP \rightarrow 2NH_3 + H_2 + 16ADP + 16P_i}$$
- **Atmospheric:** lightning: $\mathrm{N_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO};\ \mathrm{2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2};\ \mathrm{3NO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow 2HNO_3 + NO}$
- **Industrial:** Haber process: $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \xrightarrow{Fe} 2NH_3}$

### 2. Assimilation
Plants absorb $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ and $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ from soil; nitrate is reduced ($\mathrm{NO_3^- \rightarrow NO_2^- \rightarrow NH_4^+}$) and incorporated into amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll. Animals get organic N by eating plants.

### 3. Ammonification
On death and excretion, decomposers (bacteria like *Bacillus*, fungi) convert organic N (proteins, urea, uric acid) into ammonia:
$$\text{Proteins} \rightarrow \text{amino acids} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_3};\qquad \mathrm{CO(NH_2)_2 + H_2O \rightarrow 2NH_3 + CO_2}$$

### 4. Nitrification
Aerobic oxidation of ammonia to nitrate by chemoautotrophic bacteria:
$$\mathrm{2NH_4^+ + 3O_2 \xrightarrow{Nitrosomonas} 2NO_2^- + 2H_2O + 4H^+}$$
$$\mathrm{2NO_2^- + O_2 \xrightarrow{Nitrobacter} 2NO_3^-}$$

### 5. Denitrification
Anaerobic bacteria (*Pseudomonas*, *Thiobacillus denitrificans*) in waterlogged soils reduce nitrate back to $\mathrm{N_2}$ using it instead of $\mathrm{O_2}$:
$$\mathrm{NO_3^- \rightarrow NO_2^- \rightarrow NO \rightarrow N_2O \rightarrow N_2\uparrow}$$
This closes the cycle by returning $\mathrm{N_2}$ to the atmosphere.

### Labelled diagram (described)
- **Atmospheric $\mathrm{N_2}$** (top box).
- Downward arrows: *Lightning*, *N-fixing bacteria in root nodules*, *Industrial fixation (fertilisers)* → **Ammonia ($\mathrm{NH_4^+}$) in soil**.
- **$\mathrm{NH_4^+}$** → *Nitrosomonas* → **Nitrite ($\mathrm{NO_2^-}$)** → *Nitrobacter* → **Nitrate ($\mathrm{NO_3^-}$)** [Nitrification].
- **$\mathrm{NO_3^-}$** → *absorbed by roots* → **Plants** → *eaten by* → **Animals** [Assimilation].
- **Plants and animals** → *death, excreta* → **Decomposers** → **$\mathrm{NH_3}$** [Ammonification].
- **$\mathrm{NO_3^-}$** → *Denitrifying bacteria* → upward arrow to **$\mathrm{N_2}$** [Denitrification]; side arrow *Leaching to groundwater*.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What is the main objective of Green Chemistry?
items.answer_md: The main objective of green chemistry is to **reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances** in the design, manufacture and use of chemical products, that is, to **prevent pollution at its source** (instead of treating waste afterwards) while saving energy and raw materials, so that chemistry becomes safe and sustainable.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: State and Explain three major Principles of Green Chemistry with relevant examples.
items.answer_md:
**1. Prevention (Principle 1)**
*Statement*: It is better to prevent waste than to treat or clean up waste after it is formed.
*Explanation*: Waste treatment costs money and energy and never removes all hazard; designing the process so no waste forms is cheaper and safer. The **E-factor** (kg waste / kg product) measures this.
*Example*: The BHC route to ibuprofen produces far less waste than the Boots route, and its only by-product (acetic acid) is recovered.

**2. Atom economy (Principle 2)**
*Statement*: Synthetic methods should maximise the incorporation of all materials used into the final product.
*Explanation*: $\%\ \text{AE} = \dfrac{M_\text{desired product}}{\sum M_\text{reactants}} \times 100$. Addition and rearrangement reactions have 100% AE; substitution and elimination reactions waste atoms.
*Example*: Diels-Alder reaction of butadiene and ethylene to cyclohexene: 100% AE. Ethanol to ethylene + water: $28/46 = 60.9\%$.

**3. Catalysis (Principle 9)**
*Statement*: Catalytic reagents (as selective as possible) are superior to stoichiometric reagents.
*Explanation*: A catalyst is not consumed, is used in small amounts, can be recycled, lowers the energy needed and improves selectivity, so less waste forms.
*Example*: Zeolite catalysts in petroleum cracking; enzymes (lipases) in ester synthesis; Pd catalyst in the BHC ibuprofen carbonylation.

(Equally acceptable: safer solvents, e.g. supercritical $\mathrm{CO_2}$ for decaffeination; renewable feedstocks, e.g. PLA from corn starch.)

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 1.pdf
items.question_md: What does term "Sustainability" means? Discuss any three commandments of sustainability.
items.answer_md:
**Sustainability** means using resources and the environment in a way that meets present needs without exhausting them for the future. The Brundtland Report (*Our Common Future*, **1987**) defines sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs". It rests on three pillars: **environmental, economic and social** (planet, profit, people).

**Any three commandments of sustainability**
1. **Conserve and use resources efficiently**: use renewable resources no faster than they regenerate and non-renewables sparingly, within the Earth's carrying capacity (for example, water harvesting, efficient irrigation).
2. **Reduce, reuse and recycle**: minimise waste so that it is produced no faster than nature can absorb it (segregation, composting, recycling of metals and plastics).
3. **Shift to renewable energy and save energy**: replace fossil fuels with solar, wind, hydro and biomass, and use efficient appliances, to cut pollution and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions.

(Others: prevent pollution at source, protect biodiversity, stabilise population, sustainable agriculture, intra- and inter-generational equity, clean technology and the precautionary principle, environmental education and public participation.)

items.question_md: Give reason: Percentage of Nitrogen in our atmosphere is extremely high as compared to other gases. Why?
items.answer_md:
Nitrogen is about **78%** of air because:
1. $\mathrm{N_2}$ is **chemically inert** (strong $\mathrm{N\equiv N}$ triple bond, 946 kJ/mol), so it is hardly consumed by reactions with rocks or living things, unlike $\mathrm{O_2}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$; it is also poorly soluble in water.
2. It has been released steadily for billions of years by volcanic outgassing and by **denitrifying bacteria**, and it is heavy enough (M = 28) not to escape to space; so it has accumulated while only a little is fixed by lightning and bacteria.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Give reason: Why ozone gas is present at a particular height and not evenly throughout the atmosphere?
items.answer_md:
Ozone forms by $\mathrm{O_2 + h\nu\ (\lambda < 242\ nm) \rightarrow 2O}$ and $\mathrm{O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M}$, which needs **both** short-wavelength UV and enough $\mathrm{O_2}$ and third-body (M) molecules.

- **High up (above about 35 km)**: plenty of UV, but the air is too thin for O atoms to meet $\mathrm{O_2}$ and M.
- **Low down (below about 15 km)**: plenty of $\mathrm{O_2}$, but the UV below 242 nm has already been absorbed above.

Only at about 15-35 km (stratosphere) are both met, so the ozone layer sits there.

items.topic: Sources and effects of air pollutants
items.question_md: Give reason: Why Particulate matter is considered as an Air pollutant?
items.answer_md:
Particulate matter (PM) is an air pollutant because these fine solid or liquid particles suspended in air harm health and the environment:
- $\mathrm{PM_{10}}$ lodges in the nose and throat, and $\mathrm{PM_{2.5}}$ penetrates deep into the alveoli and even the blood, causing asthma, bronchitis, heart disease and lung cancer.
- They carry adsorbed toxins (heavy metals, PAHs), reduce visibility (haze, smog), soil buildings and block leaf stomata, reducing photosynthesis.

items.topic: Control of gaseous and particulate pollutants
items.question_md: Explain the function and structure of catalytic converter in an automobile, with the help of a clear diagram.
items.answer_md:
**Function**: a catalytic converter, fitted in the exhaust line between the engine and the silencer, converts the toxic exhaust gases CO, unburnt hydrocarbons (HC) and $\mathrm{NO_x}$ into harmless $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$.

**Structure (diagram described)**: a stainless-steel shell with exhaust inlet from the engine and outlet to the silencer. Label inside:
- **Substrate**: a ceramic (cordierite) honeycomb monolith with thousands of fine parallel channels, giving a large surface.
- **Washcoat**: porous $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ (with $\mathrm{CeO_2}$ as oxygen store) coated on the channels.
- **Catalyst**: thin layer of noble metals, Pt and Pd (oxidation) and Rh (reduction).
- Heat-resistant mat holding the monolith, and an oxygen ($\lambda$) sensor before the converter.

**Reactions (three-way converter)**
- Oxidation: $\mathrm{2CO + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2}$; $\mathrm{C_xH_y + (x + \tfrac{y}{4})O_2 \rightarrow xCO_2 + \tfrac{y}{2}H_2O}$
- Reduction: $\mathrm{2NO + 2CO \rightarrow N_2 + 2CO_2}$

It works best at about 400-800 °C and an air-fuel ratio near 14.7:1. **Leaded petrol must not be used**, because lead poisons the catalyst; this is why unleaded petrol was introduced.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: What is lapse rate? Explain the reason why positive lapse rate is found in troposphere whereas Stratosphere follows negative lapse rate.
items.answer_md:
**Lapse rate**: the rate of decrease of air temperature with increase in altitude,
$$\Gamma = -\frac{dT}{dz}$$
It is **positive** when temperature falls with height and **negative** when temperature rises with height (inversion). Normal value in the troposphere is about **6.5 °C/km**.

**Positive lapse rate in the troposphere**: the troposphere is heated **from below**. Sunlight passes through the air and heats the Earth's surface, which then warms the air above it by conduction, convection and IR radiation. Moving away from this heat source the air becomes cooler; also rising air expands at lower pressure and cools adiabatically. So temperature falls with height (15 °C to about -56 °C).

**Negative lapse rate in the stratosphere**: the stratosphere contains the **ozone layer**, which absorbs solar UV and releases heat:
$$\mathrm{O_3 + h\nu\ (UV) \rightarrow O_2 + O,\qquad O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M + heat}$$
UV intensity, and so heating, is greatest at the top, so temperature increases with height (about -56 °C to about -2 °C).

items.topic: Control of gaseous and particulate pollutants
items.question_md: Explain the principle behind Electrostatic Precipitators to remove air pollution.
items.answer_md:
**Principle**: particles are charged by a corona discharge and then collected on an oppositely charged surface by electrostatic attraction.

1. **Corona and ion generation**: a high negative DC voltage (30-100 kV) is applied to thin discharge wires placed between earthed collecting plates. The strong field near the wire ionises gas molecules (corona), producing electrons and negative ions.
2. **Particle charging**: as dusty gas flows through, the negative ions attach to the particles, which become negatively charged.
3. **Migration and collection**: the electric field drives charged particles to the earthed plates, where they are neutralised and held.
4. **Removal**: plates are rapped (or washed) and the dust falls into a hopper; clean gas leaves.

Efficiency is above 99% for particles down to about 0.1 µm, with low pressure drop; $\eta = 1 - e^{-wA/Q}$. Used in thermal power plants, cement and steel plants. It cannot remove gaseous pollutants.

items.topic: Sources and effects of air pollutants
items.question_md: What is the impact of $CO_2$ and $CH_4$ in Global Warming? Discuss its causes and preventive measures.
items.answer_md:
**Global warming** is the rise in the Earth's average surface temperature due to an enhanced greenhouse effect: greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit part of it back to the surface.

**Impact of $\mathrm{CO_2}$**
- Concentration has risen from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to ~420 ppm today.
- Contributes about 60% of the enhanced greenhouse effect because of its large amount and long life (centuries), although its GWP is only 1.
- Also dissolves in oceans forming carbonic acid, causing **ocean acidification** and coral bleaching.

**Impact of $\mathrm{CH_4}$**
- Concentration has more than doubled since pre-industrial times (~0.7 to ~1.9 ppm).
- Per molecule about **28 times** more effective than $\mathrm{CO_2}$ over 100 years (GWP ~28); contributes about 20% of warming; lifetime ~12 years.

**Causes**
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | $\mathrm{CH_4}$ |
|---|---|
| Burning of coal, oil and natural gas in power plants, vehicles and industry | Paddy (rice) fields: anaerobic decay |
| Deforestation (fewer trees to absorb $\mathrm{CO_2}$) and burning of forests | Enteric fermentation in cattle (ruminants) |
| Cement manufacture: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2}$ | Landfills and sewage (anaerobic decomposition) |
| Burning of crop residue and waste | Leaks from coal mines, natural gas pipelines; melting permafrost |

**Consequences (brief)**: melting glaciers, sea-level rise, extreme weather, crop loss, spread of diseases, species loss.

**Preventive measures**
1. Shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro) and nuclear; improve energy efficiency.
2. Afforestation and stopping deforestation to increase carbon sinks; carbon capture and storage.
3. Public transport, electric vehicles, fuel-efficient engines.
4. Methane control: capture landfill gas and biogas from dung for fuel; better paddy water management (alternate wetting and drying); improved cattle feed; stop gas leaks.
5. Carbon tax and carbon credits; international agreements (Kyoto Protocol 1997, Paris Agreement 2015).
6. Reduce, reuse, recycle; awareness.

items.topic: Sources and effects of air pollutants
items.question_md: What are the major sources of Indoor Air pollution. How can indoor pollution be prevented?
items.answer_md:
**Indoor air pollution** is the contamination of air inside homes, offices and schools; since people spend ~90% of their time indoors, it is often more harmful than outdoor pollution.

**Major sources**
| Source | Pollutants released |
|---|---|
| Cooking and heating with wood, dung, coal, kerosene (chulhas) | CO, particulate matter, $\mathrm{NO_2}$, PAHs |
| Tobacco smoking | CO, nicotine, benzene, PAHs, formaldehyde |
| Building materials and furniture (plywood, particle board, adhesives, paints, insulation) | formaldehyde, VOCs, asbestos fibres |
| Soil and rocks below the building, granite | radon (radioactive) |
| Household products (cleaners, air fresheners, mosquito coils, pesticides, cosmetics) | VOCs, particulates |
| Damp walls, AC ducts, carpets, pets | biological pollutants: mould, bacteria, dust mites, pollen |
| Gas stoves and heaters | $\mathrm{NO_2}$, CO |

**Prevention**
1. **Ventilation**: cross-ventilation, chimneys and exhaust fans (kitchen hoods) to remove smoke and gases.
2. **Cleaner fuels**: replace wood and dung with LPG, PNG, biogas or electricity (Ujjwala scheme); use improved smokeless chulhas.
3. **No smoking indoors**.
4. **Low-emission materials**: low-VOC paints, formaldehyde-free furniture, avoid asbestos.
5. **Radon control**: seal floor cracks, sub-slab ventilation, test radon levels.
6. **Moisture control**: fix leaks, keep humidity low, clean AC filters to stop mould.
7. **Air purifiers and indoor plants** (money plant, snake plant, areca palm) to remove particulates and VOCs.
8. **Safe use of household chemicals**: use in ventilated areas, store sealed; regular dusting and vacuuming.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Explain the phenomenon of Ozone hole in Stratosphere. Why is it concentrated mostly over Antarctica?
items.answer_md:
### Ozone hole
The **ozone hole** is a region of the stratosphere, appearing over Antarctica every spring (September-October), where total column ozone falls below **220 DU** (normal about 300 DU; 1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure $\mathrm{O_3}$ at STP).

### Normal balance (Chapman cycle)
- $\mathrm{O_2 + h\nu\ (\lambda < 242\ nm) \rightarrow 2O}$; $\mathrm{O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M}$
- $\mathrm{O_3 + h\nu \rightarrow O_2 + O}$; $\mathrm{O + O_3 \rightarrow 2O_2}$

### Depletion by CFCs
1. CFCs are inert and long-lived, so they reach the stratosphere, where UV splits them: $\mathrm{CF_2Cl_2 + h\nu \rightarrow CF_2Cl^\bullet + Cl^\bullet}$
2. $\mathrm{Cl^\bullet + O_3 \rightarrow ClO^\bullet + O_2}$
3. $\mathrm{ClO^\bullet + O \rightarrow Cl^\bullet + O_2}$
4. **Net**: $\mathrm{O_3 + O \rightarrow 2O_2}$; Cl is regenerated, so one Cl destroys about $10^5$ $\mathrm{O_3}$ molecules. Bromine from halons acts the same way and is even more effective.

Normally most Cl is locked in inactive reservoirs: $\mathrm{Cl + CH_4 \rightarrow HCl + CH_3}$ and $\mathrm{ClO + NO_2 \rightarrow ClONO_2}$.

### Why it is concentrated over Antarctica
1. **Polar vortex**: during the dark polar winter a strong circumpolar wind isolates the air mass over Antarctica, so it cannot mix with warmer, ozone-rich air.
2. **Extreme cold and PSCs**: temperatures drop below about -78 °C and **polar stratospheric clouds** of ice and nitric acid form. Antarctica is much colder than the Arctic, so PSCs are far more common there.
3. **Chlorine activation on PSCs**: $\mathrm{HCl + ClONO_2 \rightarrow Cl_2 + HNO_3}$ and $\mathrm{ClONO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HOCl + HNO_3}$. $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ stays in the cloud particles (denitrification), so no $\mathrm{NO_2}$ is left to lock ClO back up.
4. **Spring sunlight**: in September $\mathrm{Cl_2 + h\nu \rightarrow 2Cl^\bullet}$ and $\mathrm{HOCl + h\nu \rightarrow OH + Cl^\bullet}$ release a burst of Cl, and the ClO dimer cycle ($\mathrm{2ClO \rightarrow Cl_2O_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2O_2 + h\nu \rightarrow Cl + ClOO}$, $\mathrm{ClOO \rightarrow Cl + O_2}$) destroys ozone rapidly.
5. In November-December the vortex breaks down, ozone-rich air mixes in and the hole fills.

The Arctic vortex is weaker and warmer, so Arctic loss is smaller and irregular.

**Consequence**: more UV-B reaches the surface (skin cancer, cataract, damage to phytoplankton and crops). **Control**: Montreal Protocol (1987) phasing out CFCs and halons.

items.question_md: What is the significance of grit chamber in preliminary step of waste water treatment?
items.answer_md:
The **grit chamber** is a preliminary-treatment unit placed after screens and before the primary sedimentation tank. It is a narrow channel in which the flow velocity is kept at about **0.3 m/s**, slow enough for heavy inorganic particles (sand, gravel, cinders, specific gravity about 2.65) to settle in 1-2 min, but fast enough to keep lighter organic matter in suspension.

**Significance:**
1. Protects pumps, pipes and mechanical equipment from **abrasion and wear**.
2. Prevents **clogging** of pipes and channels.
3. Prevents accumulation of inert grit in primary tanks and **sludge digesters**, which would reduce their useful volume.
4. Makes the later sludge more organic and easier to digest.

Settled grit is removed and used for landfilling.

items.path: library/archive/CY1110/End Term Previous Year Questions/End Term 2021-22 Sem 2.pdf
items.question_md: Explain the difference between point-source and non-point source pollution.
items.answer_md:
**Point-source pollution** is discharged into a water body from a single, identifiable and fixed location, such as a pipe, drain or outfall. Examples: effluent from a factory, outfall of a sewage treatment plant, discharge from a thermal power plant (thermal pollution). Because the source is known, it can be measured, monitored and regulated by treatment and discharge standards.

**Non-point source pollution** comes from diffuse sources spread over a large area, with no single outlet. Rain or irrigation water picks up pollutants as it runs over land or seeps into the ground. Examples: fertiliser and pesticide runoff from farms, urban runoff carrying oil and litter, sediment from construction sites, acid rain.

| Point source | Non-point source |
|---|---|
| Single identifiable outlet | Many diffuse sources |
| Continuous, predictable | Intermittent, depends on rainfall |
| Easy to monitor and treat | Hard to monitor; controlled by land-use practices |
